utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're told that there's some difficulty about getting the witnesses here this morning. They're in a traffic jam.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, so I understand. Might the time first be used conveniently to deal with the application in respect of Neill Wright.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position has been set out in our motion of the admission of his evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, dated the 22nd of March of 2002. I trust that the Chamber has had both the statement and an opportunity to consider the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the absence thus far of reaction by the accused or, I think, the amici, I will simply remind the Chamber that the -- and for those who will be observing the trial, that the statement produces various statistical material provided to a human rights organisation and, in particular, deals extensively with numbers of displaced persons. The formal requirements of Rule 92 bis have been complied with so that the Chamber is left to consider its discretion guided, as that discretion is, by factors listed in 92(A)(i) and (ii). It is our case that the evidence is cumulative in nature because other witnesses have given oral evidence of similar facts, and, indeed, Patrick Ball has dealt with statistics to a broadly similar effect and has relied on the material produced by the proposed 92 bis witness so that it's corroborative of two types of evidence that the Chamber has already admitted and considered. As to cross-examination, we would respectfully invite you to say that although it's of course a matter for discretion, in this particular case the accused's cross-examination has been not to the fact of displacement but to the motivation or cause of it, and therefore, that doesn't bring him with any of the tests automatically giving him a right to cross-examination, it remaining a matter of discretion for the Chamber. Your Honours, perhaps that summarises the position for the time being and I'll await what, if any, reactions are there for me to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, perhaps you could deal with one or two matters. The first is attachment number five, the statement of Mrs. Ogata made to a working group on the 6th of April, 1999. I'm not sure that it adds very much in any event, and it speaks of forced displacement and the like, and I don't think we need be minded in any event to admit that through this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. She's been referred to in evidence very recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps more important would be, accepting for the moment your argument that really what is being dealt with by this witness is the statistics, the fact that there were refugees, which hasn't been disputed, the issue being as to why there were -- why there was displacement, attachment four, just the emergency update, that is the day-to-day reports, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And this witness is in Colombo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sri Lanka, I think, at the moment, but he is available. I'm not pretending that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. But if he was forced to give evidence, he would come rather a long way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He would indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But that's, of course, not a compelling factor, just a practical matter. Yes. Thank you. We'll hear from the amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've not identified any further issue that might assist the Court except for one; that is, we believe that the accused does have the right of cross-examination if he wishes to do so. And that's the only observation we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we're dealing with the statement of Mr. Neill Wright. His statement has been served. He is a witness from the UNHCR who deals with displacement. And the point the Prosecution make in asking that the statement be admitted, and without cross-examination, is that what he deals with is the statistics of displacement. He does not deal with the reasons for it, that being the -- that latter being the issue in the case. Now, is there anything you want to say to us about that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have a chance of seeing his testimony, his statement, and as he's not on the list of the next 30-odd witnesses, this is very far in advance, and I don't go that far in advance, of course. So I don't know anything about his statement or testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His statement was served with the Prosecution motion of the 22nd of March. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two matters we have to deal with. The first is this: Mr. Milosevic has not addressed us on the issue, saying he hasn't read the papers. But the fact is this: that this motion was served as long ago as the 22nd of March. We bear in mind that he is representing himself and there are a large number of papers. It is therefore more difficult than it would be in a simple case or more difficult than it would be for an accused who is represented. All that we bear in mind. But nonetheless, he had notice that this matter was to be dealt with. He had notice on Friday that we would be dealing with it this morning. So he had every opportunity to read the papers and be in a position to address us. He hasn't taken that opportunity. We deal with it on the basis that his reaction would be similar to his reaction to other such motions for the admission of written statements, namely, that he would wish to cross-examine the witness, and on that basis, we consider the motion. We will admit this statement under Rule 92 bis. It is of cumulative nature since it deals with the statistics of displacement. There has been evidence from many witnesses about the fact of displacement. There has been evidence from Dr. Ball about the statistics of displacement. Therefore, this evidence is cumulative of other evidence and is admissible. We do not consider that cross-examination in this case is necessary, in the exercise of our discretion, since the witness deals purely with the fact of displacement and not with the reasons for it. There has been no issue that people were displaced. The issue has been: Why were they displaced? The statement will be admitted as evidence of the statistics of displacement and the fact that people were displaced. It will not be admitted as evidence of why they were displaced. And in any event, attachment 5, the statement of Mrs. Ogata, will be excluded. It would not be admissible through this witness in any event, and it deals much more closely with the issue which we've identified, namely, the reasons for displacement, which is a matter which is very much in dispute. Accordingly, we admit the statement under Rule 92 bis. We exclude attachment 5, Mrs. Ogata's speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. I'm not sure whether the witness has yet arrived. If not, there's another procedural matter that I can raise and make use of the time in doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is the witness here?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They have arrived, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something precisely with respect to the statistics you were talking about. Statistics can serve a purpose if it deals with the facts introduced and if those facts are correct, if it deals with the correct facts and figures. But in the practice so far this has not -- here, this has not been the case. We heard the testimony that you mentioned a moment ago by Patrick Ball, for example, which I wholly challenged. And secondly, we are not talking about displacement. And I don't know what you imply by using the term "displacement," because just one thing is without a doubt and that is that there were refugees who had fled, fled from the places where there lived due to the war. Now, if statistics -- if the statistics is about statistics related to refugees, then we can only look at it if the input is correct, the facts are correct, and not -- it does not apply to any displacement that is not connected to refugees. Refugees and war are two things that have always been linked, two phenomena that have also been linked. There has been no war without refugees or refugees without war, as far as I know anything on the subject. So we're talking about - how shall I put it? - an endeavour, I think, to have the reasons for some sort of displacement ascribed to some other elements and points in time, intentions, plans that we have been listening to here the whole time but never anything than rumours and hearsay, people having heard about something. And that is why I think that statistical presentations of this kind, in my opinion, can be qualified as being worthless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've ruled, Mr. Milosevic, and you've heard the reasons for our ruling. Yes, we'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as I say, I see that we have a little time. May I just say that my telephone isn't working again. I don't know how many times this telephone, which is supposed to be at my disposal, is out of order and I can't use it because it's not working, it's not operational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have that looked into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Salihi, we'll conclude your evidence now. You'll remember the declaration that you gave on Friday, which of course still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to continue your cross-examination. It appears that there are about 40 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't need as much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salihi, in your statement, it says that you heard, when the events that you described took place, that in the Serbian language somebody said, "There are terrorists here." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, you said that in your village there were no members of the KLA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there haven't been any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the close vicinity, right next to your village, in the villages of Bela Crkva, Zrze, Mala Krusa, Pirana, Medvedza, Samodreza, Studencane, Zociste, that in those villages there were members of the KLA and their groups present?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of any occurrence taking place nearby your village, such as an abduction or killing or anything else that might have happened in those villages? Did you hear anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've heard about it when we've heard that Serbian forces have gone in and killed people, slayed them. They've done everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you heard of events and occurrences when -- involving KLA members, when the KLA members perpetrated crimes in the villages around your village, the villages I enumerated.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At -- there's been -- there's been no KLA in Celine, and this question is not for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Celine. I'm talking about what you say you heard and if you heard anything from the surrounding villages, and I'm talking about what we're referring to as the KLA, that organisation.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not heard anything about any KLA or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you think that they might have come into conflict in those villages, clashes, and that a group of KLA members fled towards your village and that they were following that group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said that he knows nothing about the KLA in the surrounding villages, and that's his answer. He can't add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness doesn't know anything with respect to the KLA. He just knows one side - that's quite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clear - one side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your written statement that the policemen, according to what it says here, had assault rifles. What do you mean when you say "assault rifles"? What are they?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian forces came into the village of Celine and they did everything against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about rifles. You said that they had assault rifles.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say what kind of weapons they had, but Celine came under shelling. And we were not there in the business of going out into the open for them to shell us, and then that's exactly what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph -- I'm asking you a specific question. On page 2, in the middle of this paragraph -- I only have the text in English and I'm going to read the sentence. [In English] "I can't remember anything about badges on their uniforms. These policemen were armed with assault rifles." [Interpretation] That's what I'm asking you. What makes these rifles different from other rifles? What are assault rifles, since you claim that they carried some kind of assault rifles?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had -- [indiscernible] automatic guns. This is some kind of a grammatical exercise, and I'm no good at grammar of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not twisting anything. I'm just reading what's been written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we see what's in the statement. The witness has answered as best he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it all boils down to the following: Your village, until the 25th of March - and that is the date on which this event occurred that you described - it was a peaceful village and there were no incidents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 25th, there was nothing of the kind. After that, we came under siege and the Serbs did what they always wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that on the 24th of March, the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia started, that war started?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know this, and that is the reason why Serbian forces besieged us and threw all their revenge upon us, because we were very happy that NATO intervened, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So until the end -- the beginning of the war, it was peaceful, and you did not have any problems; and then when the war began, the events that usually accompany a war started. Do you ascribe everything that happened to the war or to something else?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened upon the civilians by the Serbian forces only -- can only be laid at their door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I hope that we are clear on one thing, and that is that until the beginning of the war, there were no events of this kind whatsoever; all the trouble began when the war began. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only one question arising from last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Salihi, you've told us about people being killed in your village. How many people were killed, roughly, or exactly, if you can help us?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that exactly. Until the 25th or the 28th, I can explain everything here, because I've got everything here in my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many people? Just tell us that.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seventy-five in the village of Celine, aged from 1 year old to 90 year old. They were all killed and massacred in their own households.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I should explain that this witness, as several witnesses do, come to Court with photographs and documentation that they think will help us. It's always a balance as to whether we should take time producing that material. With this particular witness, although he produced the material, it seemed to me that his witness statement dealt with matters, and I don't ask for it to be produced in evidence. But they bring this material, as this witness did, hoping that they can help the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Salihi. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now finished and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness comes, and because I'm not going to be here after the break, myself, until next week, I wonder if I could explain one or two procedural matters in a way that I hope will help the Chamber and set out the way we're going to deal with things from now on. I hope that will be convenient. It will take about five minutes or perhaps a little longer. I hope that's acceptable. Your Honour, we're now in a position, prosecuting this case in the three indictments, to take account of all decisions that this Chamber has made, indeed the Appeals Chamber's decision in relation to joinder, and we can take account of the experience of the time being taken, for example, with the 92 bis witnesses. And we obviously have our concerns. First of all, we appreciate that there are, or may be, different views about how long these trials should take, or this trial should take, in particular how much time should be taken by crime-base evidence. And although the Prosecution will, and does, hold to its view of what's appropriate, reflected in the list of witnesses we've served, it would be quite wrong of us not to take account of the views of others, as expressed or implied, to respect them, and to recognise that of course our view may well be wrong. We don't believe it's wrong, but we must take that view and we must respond to those possibilities. Now that we can work out how long evidence in the Kosovo limb will take, the evidence that we've served, we've done the statistics, and if we were to call the evidence listed and on the most favourable assumptions that, for example, four 92 bis witnesses a day and live crime-base witnesses half a day, and experts and internationals one and a half days - you can do it various ways - the time that would be taken would take us well beyond the break, into October. It appears to us that there are only a few remaining issues that can affect the length of time that need final resolution. I'll identify them and ask to say one or two words about one or two of them in a second. There's the binders, what use may be made of them; there's the cross-examination of amici, which is being dealt with by a separate motion; and then there's the final position of summarising witnesses. I'll come back to two of those shortly. But in light of the statistics as we've understood them - and of course those statistics are in line with the original time estimates given by the Prosecutor and by myself on earlier occasions - we've decided to re-order the witnesses to give a priority not to the crime-base witnesses now, or at least after this week, but, wherever possible, to the other witnesses; the internationals, insiders, and the witnesses of linkage. What we intend to do is to get as many of those witnesses in as soon as may be. This, to some degree, disrupts the order and presentation of evidence, but we think that's a necessary course to take, and we'll keep 92 bis witnesses in reserve - we hope not at their inconvenience - so that they can fill gaps as gaps may appear if we have trouble, as we may well do, getting these witnesses from around the world to come sooner than had originally been planned. We don't yet know, incidentally, what is the outcome of the Kosovo interpretation booth dilemma, but if -- we hope that this won't waste interpretation booth time if it's limited, we've got that in mind, but nevertheless, we have to have in mind the overall time scale. Now, merely calling those witnesses early isn't going to solve the problem if there is a problem between the time that we believe is required and the time that the Chamber has allowed, and so I intend to do the following in respect to basically all witnesses in this trial unless I'm told not to, and all witnesses in all parts of the trial: I will take steps where possible to have their evidence in chief admitted under the provisions of 92 bis, and that will apply for all witnesses. I will come to detail of that, but before I do, the accused has been saying that from time to time that having witness statements as evidence in chief is not known to any system of law. I haven't bothered to correct him because when he says things that are wrong, if I stand up to correct them, it always takes time. He's quite wrong about that. Just to take one jurisdiction, the English, in all cases that are not criminal in nature, including the large commercial cases that attract litigation from around the world, I believe, as Your Honour will know, examination-in-chief has been a thing of the past for years. All evidence is adduced by the way of production and adoption of written statements. And of course there are plenty of arguments that one can deploy for saying that this sort of litigation is much more like large civil litigation with professional Judges and big, detailed issues of the type that are handled by both the small civil courts in England or the large courts that deal with banking and other associated matters and so on. So he's quite wrong in saying that this is without precedent. It's absolutely with precedent, and it's been recognised as a technique for saving time, certainly in England and I expect around the world. And of course what happens is exactly what Your Honours have allowed in the case of these 92 bis witnesses; that the witness adopts his statement as accurate and is allowed a few questions of -- to settle him in, maybe one or two matters of detail covered, and than he is exposed or she is exposed to cross-examination. So it seems to us if there is going to be problems of getting a sufficient quantity of evidence in within the time allowed, that we must use every available technique to abbreviate time. And of course, not having evidence in chief is not something that we want, but it's something that we think we can certainly live with. But it would require some constructive use of 92 bis, which has its own provisions. As the Chamber will recall, 92 bis may only apply in respect of evidence of a witness which goes to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused. So that any statement that deals and only deals with such matter, it seems to us, probably couldn't qualify under 92 bis. But there is another part of 92 bis that is of value. 92 bis (E), I think, which says that: "... The Trial Chamber shall decide, after hearing the parties, whether to admit the statement or transcript in whole or in part and whether to require the witness to appear for cross-examination." So that if there are statements from witnesses -- and I'll come to the other difficulties that arise in relation to this possible technique, but if there are statements that in part deal with acts of the accused and in part deal with other background matter, then, and entirely sensibly, it should be to partition the witness's statement up. I don't mean physically, but to say, Well, as to paragraphs 1 to 10, admitted under 92 bis with entitlement of the accused to cross-examine; as to paragraphs 11 to 20, which deal with acts of the accused, well, that will have to be given in chief in the regular way. So it seems to us that if I can bring ourselves within the provisions of 92 bis for any witness, for all witnesses, then this will save a great deal of time. Of course, it won't be possible to go around the world and go through the process of 92 bis'ing, as it's rather unelegantly called, or inelegantly called, every conceivable witness, but witnesses, when they come here, of course go through their existing statements which have been served on the accused and the amici, and if they simply adopt the statement as accurate, it can then be taken to the independent limb of the Registry who can deal with the attesting process that makes the statement potentially valid before this Chamber. If the witness wishes to add to or to amend or correct the statement, a second statement could be taken and that statement can itself be taken through the 92 bising process. Now, if that happens, there will be potential difficulties arising from the notice provisions set out in 92 bis (E), because, of course, statements have to have 14 days' notice to the opposing party for provision of seven days' objection. Well, it's always open to the Chamber Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to abbreviate time. If the statement in substance or the statement has been served in advance on the accused, as they all have been, there would be no prejudice to him, especially if the Chamber were to decide to allow the statement in, in whole or part, subject to cross-examination. And so we might find ourselves in the position again -- unless the Chamber rejects this altogether as a useful technique, we might find ourselves in the position of saying, well, as forecast, Witness X is available today or tomorrow. His statements have been attested to under the provisions of 92 bis and we would ask the whole statement to go in as his evidence, subject to such cross-examination as the Chamber may allow. Alternatively, if the statement is one where certain paragraphs could not qualify under the opening provisions of 92 bis, we'd say the Chamber should have the whole statement, there being no embarrassment in the Chamber having the whole statement, other Chambers do, but we would seek to apply the provisions of 92 bis to the parts that don't specifically concern the conduct of the accused. There's one other potential difficulty, and this is a procedure and I've tried to think of all problems in advance and alert the Chamber to them, and it's to do with the language of the statements, given the problems of translation that we have. What happens at the moment is that the witnesses come in, their statements, which have been served on the accused in English and in B/C/S, are then subject to review and the proofing summaries that are served are prepared, but they're only prepared in English because they're not -- it's not possible to prepare them in B/C/S in the time available, and they are, of course, a voluntary provision in excess of our duties. We now know better than the Chamber did when the matter was raised earlier, that the accused speaks English to a very high level, and we would invite the Chamber to say that it would be possible in these circumstances again to be satisfied that there is no prejudice in the provision of 92 bis statements in this way. So, Your Honour, it has yet to be seen how it operates in practice. Of course the Chamber may rule against us, but I hope it won't. But it does seem to us that this is a technique that will save some more time, be consistent with modern practice, and the Chamber will always be able to afford the accused the opportunity to cross-examine, which is what is important to him, even though the Prosecution will lose that which they normally value, which is the opportunity for their cases to be given in public. With that in mind, I'll therefore give oral notice now that it's our intention to -- under this method, to seek to rely on the provisions of 92 bis for any and every witness forthcoming, and I'll deal with the details witness-by-witness as we are able to provide revised witness lists, but I hope that that notice will serve a purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think what you propose to do is quite interesting, but it seems to me that there is a certain basic screening that should be done by the Prosecution in this exercise rather than throwing everything at the Chamber, every possible witness. The Prosecution should itself do some screening, because there's no point putting any and every witness up for 92 bis if the very basic requirements are not met. The evidence must purport to go to matters other than the acts and conduct of the accused, and then the provision also sets out some indicia as to admissibility. So if you have a witness whose testimony doesn't meet those basic criteria, why put up that witness? So while I find it interesting, I believe that there's an onus on the Prosecutor to do what I call this very basic screening. Because what you propose is really an indiscriminate exercise in which any and every witness will be put up as a possible 92 bis, and I believe that you should be a little more selective.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I certainly wasn't seeking rulings today. I was simply trying to give the Chamber an indication of what was in my mind, as I always do, so that the Chamber can think ahead and dwell on these matters. And of course, there may be witnesses who don't qualify at all because they are all about the acts of the accused, in which case, of course, we wouldn't put them in. And as to screening, of course we're screening witnesses. We're very mindful of the additional burden that this exercise will place on everyone. There's no need to expose people to unnecessary labours if it's simply wasted. So of course we'll be reviewing each witness on a witness-by-witness basis, but this is my broad plan at the moment. So when I say I'm, as it were, giving notice that any such witness may be subject to 92 bis, that is exactly what I'm doing, and we'll review it as times comes along. And of course this will apply not only for the Kosovo limb, but in due course it will apply to the other limbs of the case. But we don't know what the timetables are going to be there, we don't know whether there will be the same pressure, for example, in Croatia, or whether it would be possible, as it would certainly be desirable in all cases, to have at least some witnesses give their evidence in chief fully. But as long as we have, and must respect and reflect, timetables that are operative on us, we have to look at all provisions, and that's why I've said that we're considering it for, and give notice that we may be considering it for, are considering it for, every witness. Can I -- because I've got a few other things to say, so that I can be entirely transparent about what our plans are and exactly how they are going to take shape - come back to what I think are the only outstanding potential timesaving issues that are not formally and finally resolved. As I say, cross-examination by the amici is on hold, because it's obviously right that that should be the subject of a written motion for them to deal with. Location binders. In light of Your Honours' ruling last week, it would appear to us, although it wasn't said in terms, that the Chamber may not be inclined to use the binders as a tool for engaging the accused in the exercise of deciding what's admitted and not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And equally, that it may be the case that the Chamber is not minded to use the binders as a way of identifying on any not collective but joint basis what evidence may be valuable. Now, if that's the case, the residual value of the binders becomes more limited, and it does, of course, picking up from His Honour Judge Robinson's point, add to the burden of work really upon the Chamber. We don't want to flood the Chamber with material to be considered unless it's for a good purpose. We can carry on with the binder exercise if the Chamber thinks that it's useful. Now, I know it's never right for an advocate to ask a tribunal any question, and I don't. So we can carry on doing it, but of course, were the Chamber to indicate that it doesn't regard that as an exercise that brings a dividend of efficiency or the saving of time, then we won't, and we'll simply adduce the evidence in line with the rulings that are to be either implied or drawn directly from the ruling in relation to the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, it might be a convenient way in which to have the evidence together in one place about a particular village rather than having it given by perhaps a series of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll carry on, pruning them down in the way that you indicated, and make them available on that basis. There is then one other outstanding issue, which hasn't been the subject of a formal ruling, and that's the issue of the summarising witness. Now, we know that from the binder concerned, the summarising witness was excluded, as it were, in consideration of the binder. We're not sure whether that amounts to a general ruling about summarising witnesses, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't yet, I think, allowed one application for summarising witnesses. Now, it may be that you have another approach in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, again, I'm hoping to set out in advance what I'm doing rather than seeking rulings today. It seems to us that there is no Appeals Chamber jurisprudence on summarising witnesses. There's practice in different Chambers that I've drawn to your attention. And it would be desirable, if there's not to be a ruling in favour of a summarising witness in this case, that there might be Appeal Chamber jurisprudence available to all of us to guide us. Because what will be the most regrettable position would be to find - any case - to find itself in a position on appeal where the sufficiency of evidence is argued and where the Appeal Chamber says, "But there was another way of getting this in," and that matter hasn't been dealt with. So what I'm proposing to do is this, probably next week: I will seek to lead a witness. It will probably be the summarising witness in Racak, and if so, we'll serve his statement upon you in advance. And that's one, because it's a particularly large site and because this is an investigator who has prepared the maps, indeed the maps we've already used with Major General Drewienkiewicz, his maps and so on. But he's been to the site and he's conducted an investigation, but his statement also does contain a summary of what witnesses have said to him. We'll then seek your ruling in relation to that witness. And if it's favourable, then we'll be pleased to adopt the policy of using such witnesses. If it's -- or not "favourable"; if it's to admit. If it's to reject, then we would ask the Chamber at that stage to certify that this was a discrete topic suitable for appellate consideration, and then we could possibly fast-track that consideration. So that one way or another we could know where we were in relation to that category of evidence, not just for this sector of the trial but for others. So with all those changes in mind - not "changes" - with all those proposals in mind, we will come at whatever the final deadline for the Kosovo sector of the trial is, to a position where we have got in, we would hope, the best evidence. Of course we'll be putting in evidence of crime base, probably start off with one per site for the killing sites, because it may be there won't be time for more, and we'll try and use 92 bis, of course, for all crime-base witnesses, as we were always going to. But we'll come to a time when we'll know how much the Prosecution's been able to adduce. We will have the advantage of those documents that I proposed using right at the beginning of the trial, documents where we fill in what aspects of the indictment are covered by particular witnesses. The Chamber will remember I proposed they might be jointly prepared. It was rejected, but I think Your Honour Judge May suggested they might be quite useful. Well, they're being prepared. We can make them available to the amici and to the accused in the meanwhile for correction or comment, things like that. But they will be available to show where there may be gaps in the evidence measured against the indictment. There will then be a residue of evidence - I can't think of any other word - the evidence we haven't been able to get in using the various techniques that are available to us, and at that stage we may, and probably will, apply for such extension of the timetable as will accommodate whichever of those witnesses, all or some, we still regarded as important to have in the case. But we'll have reached that position having done everything we can to get the maximum amount of evidence in, giving the evidence that we suspect the Chamber thinks may have a higher priority and that we can understand may have a higher priority, giving that evidence its priority. And so we'll be in a position to make any application for extension, having respected and reflected the view as to the length of time the trial should take and done everything we can. And hopefully, we won't have to make any such application. It just depends where we are by then. But, Your Honour, that is a completely open and transparent explanation of what I propose. The same overall procedure can then follow for Croatia and Bosnia. I had no hesitation in deciding that for this case, crime-base evidence had to come first, not least because I could see there would be a range of procedural problems that would need to be sorted out, and that if we put crime-base to the end of any projected time period for trial, it would be too late, given the difficulties of amassing the witnesses and so on, gathering witnesses, it would be too late to deal with them. Well, we've now identified the problems, the potential solutions, and so on. So in Croatia and Bosnia, it will probably be the case that we'll call crime-base evidence later and the other evidence earlier, and in each case, or in each part of the case, when we come to the end of such allotted time as there may be, we'll be able again to see what residue of evidence it's not been possible for us to accommodate and make our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. decision as to whether we seek any extension of the time. In Bosnia, of course, as the Chamber well knows, there are already in hand steps - you don't take steps in hand - there are already in hand various processes for reducing the amount of time that the Prosecution would seek, in any event, by consideration of the municipalities and how many of them have to be proved to the full extent, and the Chamber will also know that there are also time-saving procedures in contemplation, time-saving not just for this trial but for all the Bosnian trials, including the Plavsic/Krajisnik trial. And of course in the Bosnia case, there are other potential time-saving mechanisms available to us by incorporating, if we may, by 92 bis, evidence in other cases, possibilities that don't arise in Kosovo or, barely, in Croatia. So that's what we're doing, and I hope it's helpful to know it in advance. We will -- this week we'll carry on with 92 bis witnesses, and, it may be, next week, because I don't know how soon we'll be able to get other witnesses here. But we will be reordering our priority of witnesses and taking the steps I've outlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two matters arising about timetabling. At the moment, the order is for 90 witnesses, so if you want to extend that, you'll have to apply to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it may be the sooner that's done, the better, so we all know where we are. The second matter is this: Looking at the timetable for the summer, what we have in mind is this: that you said you would be calling linking witnesses in July, having, it's to be hoped, finished Kosovo. We think that, at the very least, the accused and the Trial Chamber should have another two weeks besides the vacation to prepare for the next parts of the trial. So we have in mind adjourning on the -- I think it would be the 19th of July, leaving two extra weeks before the recess begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's helpful to have notice of that. Our arithmetic of how long witnesses may or will take, on the best estimates, mean inevitably that the 19th of July is a date when there will be a very substantial residue of witnesses we would want to have admitted into evidence by one means or another, probably before we get to the linkage witnesses who link one case to the next, or one indictment to the next. But we'll have that date in mind as a date when proceedings may come to an end, tailor our calling of witnesses accordingly, and try and give appropriately early attention to such applications as we must make, not only for extending the number of witnesses but also when we should be looking at the residue of witnesses. The Chamber will, I think, recall that the Prosecutor herself and I - I may have said this earlier - always envisaged that the Kosovo trial would last very much longer than the time that's been available since February and until July, even without cross-examination, and of course there has now been extensive cross-examination. But in due course - but I'm not arguing points now, and certainly not taking other than, I hope, an entirely cooperative and helpful approach - the Chamber will have in mind that the way things have worked out, the accused is occupying over 50 per cent of court time and we're occupying about 45 per cent, and that's going to change dramatically with the statistics for the 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter I wanted to raise was the OSCE report, about which there was talk earlier, and as the case goes on, I think the more helpful it would be to have it. Have we got copies of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's come down most mornings, and not this morning. They will be down with you at the break. I am proposing to call the witness who can produce and give evidence of the methodology of that report. She is already on notice and she is willing to come. So we'll call her; if leave is granted, to call the additional witness at the earliest opportunity, so that methodology can be explained. The reports themselves will be available to you after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the report when it's available and we'll hear the witness in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We're not making, as you'll understand, any ruling at this stage. There's no ruling about the future of the case or about the evidence or anything of that sort. We've merely heard the Prosecution outline its plans, and we'll consider them insofar as they affect the case in due course. So no ruling has been made or is asked for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that you have not made a ruling, but I assume that, for making a ruling, it will not be too much if I say something about what Mr. Nice has been talking about. The first question relates to written submissions, written statements. He explained himself that written statements are used in cases that are not criminal cases. I'm glad to hear that, because I have been claiming anyway that this is not a criminal case. This is a political case. It's not even court proceedings from the point of view of law and justice. However, since you treat this as a criminal case, then I assume that it is quite unacceptable to introduce a practice for such considerations and for such deliberations which is not really applied anywhere. As you have emphasised several times, I'm not an expert in these matters, but during one of the breaks, I asked Mr. Kay, who is a distinguished English barrister, and I asked him if this existed in English law, and he said no, this kind of practice does not. So I imagine that the other side, the opposing party, is aware of this as well. So this idea of imposing this kind of thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There must have been a misunderstanding, Mr. Milosevic, because in English law, in criminal cases, statements, written statements, can be admitted in certain circumstances, and that applies in a great number of jurisdictions that written statements are admitted. The issue really is in a case of this sort, and we'll have to consider it when we come to your case, too, in the evidence you want to put in front of us, the issue really is: Is there such a dispute about this evidence that cross-examination should be allowed? That's what we're dealing with, the issue that we're having to answer. Because if the matters are not in dispute, there's no reason it should not be put in in written form.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everything is challenged here. Everything is in dispute, everything that this indictment brings forth. However, this effort to move on from such -- two such witnesses from regular witnesses, so to speak, is something that reveals Mr. Nice's recipe or prescription or that side of his to avoid the weaknesses that became obvious during the testimony of many of his witnesses during the examination-in-chief. In this way, he would make them invulnerable because they would only be tied to their written statements. And in this way, everything would be resolved by paper. And in this way, it would be easier for him to prove the alleged facts that he wishes to prove. I also wish to draw your attention to the following: A few minutes ago, this main deception that is called Racak is something that he heralded as a case that he will seek to prove on the basis of some kind of cumulative witnesses and on the basis of some kind of expert opinions; that is to say, on the basis of witnesses who do not know anything on their own but collected other people's statements; that is to say, on the basis of the statements of his own clerks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because he merely stated that he was going to put in an application to do this. We have not ruled -- we haven't seen the application, and we haven't ruled on it, and it is something which there's little point discussing further now, taking up time with. We'll deal with it when the application is made, and then we'll know what the application is and we can rule on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I shall only dwell on one more issue quite specific. I heard an explanation here that I will be receiving all information related to witnesses in the English language, and I simply refuse that. If that is the way to prevent the normal functioning of my associates, and at any rate a different way of proceeding would be better. So I find all of this unacceptable. He is duty-bound to give me papers in my language, and I cannot accept this, and I won't accept it. I inform you thereof in advance. It is out of goodwill that I took these statements in English and I read them in English, because it is not in my interest either for this to go on for too long. But the fact that they are duty-bound to provide all of this in the Serbian language is something that should be abided by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter we will have to rule on and consider in each case. I should say we will be sitting today from 9.00 until quarter to two. We will sit the normal 9.00 day, 9.00 morning. Mr. Wladimiroff, since we've been dealing with procedural matters, is there anything the amicus wants to add or mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at this stage. We will deal with it when it comes to a concrete proposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry you've been kept waiting. We were dealing with some procedural matters. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, you were interviewed on May -- 18 and 19 of May, 1999, by members of the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct? I think we have a problem with translation.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I have problems with the translation. Too faint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we could have the witness's full name, please, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It's Ali Hoti.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better now. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, just for the record, your full name is Ali Hoti?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: My name is Ali Hoti.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You were interviewed on 18 and 19 of May by members of the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, you gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: On the 3 of February, 2002, you attended a meeting where you appeared before an officer of the Tribunal, and at this meeting you were provided with a copy of your statement in the Albanian language, which you had the opportunity to review and confirm that all its contents are the truth of the best of your knowledge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: At this stage, I would like to formally submit the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 105.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I was born at Krusha e Madhe on 6th of April, 1961.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, I am married.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you have family, children?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I have four children.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I'm a doctor by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Have you lived all of your life in Krusha e Madhe?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, I've lived all my life at Krusha.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hoti.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will give a brief summary of the witness testimony. The witness describes the attack on the village of Krusha e Madhe, where the witness lived, on 25th of March, 1999. He describes the village Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. being surrounded by Serb troops. He saw tanks, APCs, and he will describe also the Pragas approaching the village and the village being shelled, policemen and paramilitary looting property. His own house, as well as those in the surrounding village, were burnt and destroyed. The witness describes that his family started to leave the village that day and headed for the hill which is east of the village and went to the direction of Nagafc, another village. After he had left, the rest of the population also left. The population went in separate directions. When the witness arrived in a valley, he saw about 20.000 people altogether, refugees who came from the surrounding villages. The witness describes how they were ordered by Serb police and soldiers to go back to the village of Nagafc where they were spread out in houses and stayed for several days. While in Nagafc, on the 28th of March, the witness and his family were subjected to demands for cash at gunpoint by Serb police officers. The witness describes also several incidents he heard from refugees he treated while in Nagafc. One of them, Mehmet Krasniqi, had been burned, together with 109 men, by Serb police and paramilitary. And 1st April, 1999, the witness describes that Nagafc was bombed by planes he believes to have been Serbian. The witness saw many corpses at various locations throughout the village. On 2nd of April, 1999, he joined a large convoy of Kosovo Albanians heading for Albania. On the way, people were humiliated by Serb soldiers. At the Albanian border, Serb police confiscated all documents. While taking the documents, the witness heard them saying, "Kosovo is of Serbs, go to Albania where is your place. You are not citizen of Yugoslavia any more. You do not need to come back."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with the municipality, can you, Mr. Hoti? Which municipality do you live in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the municipality of Rahovec/Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your village is right next to the villages of Bela Crkva, Celine, and Zrze; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I can't understand the translation very well. It is okay now, yes. Yes, it is near.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then after those villages, we come to the other villages of Mala Krusa, Pirana, Medvedze, Samodreza, Studencane, Zociste, and so on.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No, this is wrong. Krusha e Vogel is near in Pirana as well, but Zocishte, Samadrexha, and the others are on a completely different distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, yes. The other ones too. And do you know that in all those other villages, the ones that I mentioned, there was a considerable presence of the KLA and that, throughout the time, there was a lot of tension? There were a great deal of kidnappings, killings, and other crimes. People were beaten up and so on and so forth by the KLA. Are you aware of that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there has been a KLA presence, but not in the village where we lived because there was quite a lot of inhabitants and refugees. The KLA used to stay in its own bases, and there's been absolutely no KLA activity in the villages that you mentioned. I mean any military activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you answered a question put to you by Mr. May that you were in the municipality of Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're a doctor. You had your clinic in Velika Krusa, and it would be logical for you to know what was going on in the surrounding villages and in your municipality generally because Orahovac is a small municipality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. I will answer this question. I was a doctor, but I was never given a licence to practice by yourself. I have never worked in a state-owned practice. I've had my own practice, which I help the population of the villages around there to the best of my abilities without having had a formal licence by the organs of government, your organs of government. And my -- my freedom of movement has also been curtailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. From what you have said, you had your clinic, and you did treat the population from the surrounding villages, which means a broader area, the area in which you lived, in fact, in the Orahovac municipality. Now, on that basis, can we take it that you know about what was going on, the events that took place in the area in which you lived and which you worked, in which you treated the population?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I've treated people from Krusha e Madhe, Celine, Nagafc, and Krusha e Vogel not on a broader range, because people did not come to my practice, but they went elsewhere, to Rahovec and other villages. On those -- on those four, yes, I have been a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you graduate from the faculty of medicine?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I graduated in 1994, after the Prishtina University had been closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear what your answer means. You graduated, you say, in 1994, the faculty of medicine in Pristina; is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. I will give a longer answer. The Serbian government closed the medical faculty in 1992, and I was left without completing my final year. And then I went on in our own university, which we opened without your permission, and I graduated from the University of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you graduate at the University of Kosovo? Was that in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I said once, and I'll say it once again: In Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that throughout the time that you're talking about, during that period, the faculty of medicine functioned in Pristina, was working, and that many students studied at the faculty of medicine in Pristina? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I know very well, but I also know that the medical faculty operated only for the Serbs of Kosova and not for the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was at that faculty of medicine of the Pristina University, for which you claim functioned for the Serbs, Albanians were educated there too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No. After the closure of the faculty, we studied on other premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you explain to me, please, whether the faculty was closed or was it only the Serbs that attended the faculty and were educated there? What are you saying? I'm not clear on what you're saying. Are you saying that there was no longer a faculty of medicine at the Pristina University, or are you claiming that the medical faculty did exist but that Albanians were not students there? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I didn't say that the medical faculty didn't exist. I'm saying that the Prishtina faculty existed only for Serbian students, because the Albanians were dismissed, both staff and students, and we opened our own faculty on other premises. And in the faculty in which you're talking about, only Serbs studied and not Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me this: Do you claim that the Albanians were not allowed to enrol in the faculty? Or shall I be a -- put this in a different way: Could Albanians not enrol in the faculty at all, that faculty of medicine of the university in Pristina? Which?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: At the Prishtina medical faculty, after it was closed by your government, only Albanians who agreed to speak and study in the Serbian language, not in Albanian, only these Albanians were allowed to study at your faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must adjourn now. It's past the time for our break. Mr. Hoti, could you remember during the break not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes members of the Prosecution team. Mr. Milosevic, we have checked with the communications unit about the problem with the telephone. The problem apparently lies with the external connection to Belgrade, which is beyond the control, of course, of the Tribunal. The unit is unable to predict when the lines will be working again. So that's the answer. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we are being given copies of the OSCE report, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Those are the copies that we have available, and hopefully that will be of assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the accused has a copy, I take it? Or if not, he should be given one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe he has a copy, but I will check to make absolutely sure that he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, he has a copy, right there. He's pointing to it. So that's now been confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give me a clarification? I tried to shorten the cross-examination of the previous witness in order to leave more time for this witness, because all the witnesses are not the same. Can I count on that time or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see how we get on, see how much time you need, and we'll look at it at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Secondly, the telephone doesn't work even when you want to talk to The Hague, let alone Yugoslavia. The answer I keep getting is that the telephone is not authorised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let us go on. We've come to some facts. So there was a medical faculty at the University of Pristina, and as you say, in addition to Serbs, other students who were studying there were only Albanians, who agreed to have the curriculum taught to them in the Serb language. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I explained this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were no restrictions for Albanians. They could study medicine at the University of Pristina. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that they had to agree to the Serb curriculum, as I understand it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the curriculum that applies throughout the country. Are you aware that diplomas of Yugoslav medical faculties are easily and readily recognised in many countries precisely because of the curriculum that is taught?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I know this, but these diplomas were also accepted when Albanian teachers were there. But with the removal of Albanian teachers from the faculty, we were denied the right to study in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that at the medical faculty of the University of Pristina there were also Albanian professors?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The occasional one remained. I'm not saying there weren't any, but these were those who agreed to teach and to give reports in the Serbian language, not in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that Albanian professors were not expelled from the university.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I've already explained this once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, give me an answer to my direct question: Were Albanian professors expelled from the university or were they not expelled from the university?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The great majority of lecturers were expelled from the university, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. except for one or two, who agreed to work under the conditions that I mentioned a short time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've spent a quarter of an hour on this topic, Mr. Milosevic. It's not the crucial part of his evidence at all, which is what happened in his village. Now, can we move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I shall first move on to this subject in the narrowest possible sense, but I think this was important because of what he claimed at the very outset. If that were true, that would have meant that the Albanians' human rights were violated, and as you could see, they were not. They could study, they could teach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard the evidence about it. We don't need to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you spoke about a boy who was shot at. You were not present when they shot at him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: At the moment he was shot, I was inside, at home. But he was brought into the yard, and I was in the house and I was able to come out and give him first aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: You were not present when he was shot at? So you were not present, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the alleged killings on the other side of Velika Krusa. You also didn't see that; right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I can testify that 241 people were killed in Krusha e Madhe. Two hundred six were from Krusha e Madhe and thirty-five were refugees who had come to this village from other villages. Of these, 171 were buried, of whom 86 have been identified by name, and the remainder have remained unidentified because they were burned, and only their bones were found. And there are 120 others of whom we have no details down to the present day, whether they are alive or where they are. They are still missing, and you must be held to account for where these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's a different matter altogether. My question was that these alleged killings on the other side of Velika Krusa were something that you did not see, or did you see it?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I couldn't see everything at the same time because I am not omnipresent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, if you didn't see it, just say you didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw what I said in my statement, but not everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you present at any of the funerals or burials of the people you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about what happened to Fahredin Hoti. You didn't see that either. Is that right or is that not right? You can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I can't answer yes or no, because Dr. Fahredin Hoti was a medical doctor and was killed in the presence of the members of his family. And I can say that Fahredin Hoti is both a relative of mine and my colleague, and he was killed in the presence of the members of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't see that either.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I didn't see the actual murder, but I was present at his burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about an event in Mala Krusa in relation to Mehmed Krasniqi. You didn't see that either; right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: It's very well put in the statement. I wasn't present at the event, but after Mehmed Krasniqi got out of the place where 117 people were murdered and burned, he came to seek my aid. That's what the statement says. And the words, the account of the event, is his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What condition was Mehmet Krasniqi in when he came to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he came to the village of Nagafc to ask for help, Mehmet Krasniqi was burned all over his body, and his clothes were still wet from the blood of the people who had fallen on top of him. He was totally burned, and we had difficulty in taking the clothes from his body he was so badly burned. And also his face. We tried to cover his legs with other clothes, but when we -- when we started to take off his clothes, the flesh started to come off because of the severity of his burns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What did he tell you had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He explained in detail, after I'd given him first aid, that in the village of Krusha e Vogel, Serbian forces, together with local Serbs whom he had known, had gathered together all the men they could in one house belonging to the Batusha family, put them inside, brought straw and what we call dried maize stalks and started to fire on people. Then people fell, and two people fell on Mehmet. So Mehmet was lying there. And then they set fire to them, those people who were killed and wounded. Mehmet told me -- told me that after a short time, because of the smoke in the room, he returned to consciousness and got up, and there was nobody else around who was alive, and he got through a window and fled through the field and reached Nagafc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about the case related to Selami Elshani from Retimlje. You didn't see that either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Selami Elshani also burned in other place at Krusha e Madhe at a time when Serbian forces separated 17 people mainly from other villages and put them in a room and did exactly the same as they did in Krusha e Vogel. But fortunately, Selami was not hit by a bullet but was merely burned, even though he was much worse burned than Mehmet. And after a time, he regained consciousness and he came to Nagafc, where a refugee population was, and sought help, and I secured him what help I could. But Selami's condition was much worse than that of Mehmet. He was almost totally burned. The data I have given there is what Selami says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. My question was whether you had seen that or not. So you had not seen that; right? You are talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's not saying -- he has not said in either case that he saw these events. What he has narrated is what those who had been through them told him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is precisely what I wish to establish here. I have already mentioned seven or eight cases by now, and it is obvious that none of them were direct eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then also you talked about Celine and the church, but you didn't see anything by yourself. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I will answer this in this way, if the Court will allow me: If -- all these people who were at the scene of the incidents were all killed, so those who -- because those who were captured at the scene of the crime were -- all died. So there is no way in which we can give direct evidence of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What were you told happened in Celine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we were sheltered at the Prroni i Cilave at Nagafc, we began hearing bombing, and smoke -- plumes of smoke coming out of Celine. Nobody came to tell us anything, but we could surmise that something major was happening. After the case of Celine, Serbian forces reached Nagafc, burned a part of it but not all of it. And through our place into the valley, you went into the Krusha Mala and Nagafc, overlooking both of them, because at that time, dusk was falling and Serbian forces did not operate at night, with the occasional fire, gunfire. They paused. They usually paused overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said somewhere in your statement that the soldiers were setting the houses on fire using some kind of pistols. Did you actually see that, setting houses on fire by pistols?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: We have seen this from a distance, from the part that overlooked every single activity. After the looting of the villages, like I said, with pistols -- they were fired with pistols and the house was set on fire immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. After these many allegations that you made, I would like to read to you now what you saw personally. Again, I do not have -- I shall read what I have in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Which page is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7. Page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The second, third. [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... 1999 became the most tragic day for the people who were in Nogavac that day. It was the early morning that Nogavac was bombed. It was a real hell. While I was asleep that morning, at about 2.00 I woke up by the noise of an aeroplane. I heard that it had to be very close to the village and that it made a powerful noise. Soon after I heard the noise, I heard the big explosions. The window from the house where I was staying -- I was staying in broke and pieces from the ceiling were falling down. In the house where I was staying, only one woman was wounded. I gave her first aid and stopped her bleeding. People from the village called me to help the wounded people. When outside of the house, I saw that the houses were burning and heard that people were screaming. On my way in the village, I came across wounded people, mutilated, whose hands or legs had been cut off. In the first house where I stopped, five men had been wounded. One of them had cuts on his back and some of his ribs were broken. Another had a cut on his forehead. Another one had his arm broken because of the wall that had fallen on him. On the top of two others one of the walls had fallen down, and they had problems with breathing. Another one had died. His name was Gashi Sinan. He was the father of the one whose forehead was cut. The house where they were staying was the house of Gashi Sinan. I gave them the first aid with a few medicaments. I had continued to go into the other houses to see if I could give any help. I saw a 2-years-old child whose leg had been cut off. I saw 40 to 50-year-old man whose head had been completely destroyed and whose brains had all spread on the ground. I heard screams coming out of house, and when I arrived there, I saw that the ceiling had fallen down, and people told me that 20 persons had stayed inside the house.
