When I came close to the house, I heard that there were people still alive because I heard their screams. People outside around me were screaming also. I will take -- it would take hours to dig and take them out. It was impossible to do that because all the people in the village were scared and wanted to leave, to leave Nogavac as soon as possible. They were all afraid that Nogavac might be bombed again. The people got into their cars and left Nogavac. The 20 persons in the house must have died." [Interpretation] So you describe bombing, which is undeniable on the basis your statement. Is it clear to you that Serb aeroplanes were not doing any bombing, that this was NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Let us clarify here a little bit, because what I've described, there's no need to go over again. It is like it existed in the statement. I said we were asleep at the beginning, because it was late into the night, and we had gotten used to the noise of NATO airplanes. Ten days into the bombing, it was. NATO airplanes used to stay at high altitudes. We had never heard such an echo, such a big noise. At Nagafc, as opposed to NATO airplanes, the aircraft was flying very low, and the aircraft first went all over to the Pashtrik mountain, and after that, on its way back, it started bombing. Later on, pieces from the shells were to be found with the Cyrillic writing on them, which goes to show that these aircraft were yours and not NATO's. I am fully convinced that not unintentionally did your police keep us detained for days on end at Nagafc, where only a few houses had remained intact. There were houses with about 300 people inside. You can only envisage and then try to think of their conditions in one house. Your forces had intentionally put us and kept us in one single place, for the simple reason that they wanted to show that this was as a result of a NATO mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What the intentions of these forces were can only be assumed. But do you know that our airplanes, because of this vast air supremacy, were not flying there at all? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I did make the distinction between the NATO aircraft, which for ten days on end we had seen, and the flight of that very night, where the aircraft was flying very low. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you understand what is being interpreted for you? Do you understand the translation, that it is something that can be checked out? And it is quite clear that our planes weren't flying there at all and were therefore not able to bomb you.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: First of all, can I plead with Your Honour so that the accused does not offend me, because I do understand my own mother tongue very well. Whether the aircraft flew or not, I'm not in the military and I can't say that. I can't say whether it was your aircraft or NATO's but all I can mention here is what I've heard and what I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, without a doubt, you saw a bombing take place. Now, the question is: Do you understand that it was NATO bombing and not bombing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given his evidence. Mr. Hoti, there's no need to reply to this. He's given his evidence. He's said what he saw and heard. He can't take it any further. If you've got some contrary evidence, you can put it before us in due course, but meanwhile, there's no point arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it clear that those planes used inflammatory devices, from what you have been saying here and claiming? Because you say that many houses were on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you answer that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try very briefly. In the beginning, I said, after the bombing, pieces from the shells were found with Cyrillic writing, which I in no way can think that the NATO learned from the Serbs, with the Cyrillic script. That's why I think that this was not a result of a NATO bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help, from what you saw, whether, as it's put, inflammatory devices were used or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was 2.00 in the morning on that very night, and every one of us was not outside but inside our houses. And you can only think of the speed with which an aircraft operates. So we've not been in a position to know these things at night, at that very particular moment. Then I don't think that flames alone would be able to pull houses down without some kind of explosive device, and there have been quite a few of these houses that were pulled down this way in Nagafc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Had you seen the shells with Cyrillic writing or was that something that somebody told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said they were found later and handed over to the competent organs. I don't know who exactly. But I know that from people who told me that they had been handed over to the internationals to be verified and checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So destructive and explosive devices were used, according to what you say; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given his evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what you were talking about a moment ago, perhaps, about the people who suffered great burns, serious burns, was that perhaps also the result of the bombing in which, in addition to the destructive powers, incendiary devices were used too?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Even earlier, when I referred to the burned people, those who had been burned at Krusha e Vogel, this had happened before the bombing, some days before the bombing, at Krusha e Madhe as well. There were 68 burned persons from Krusha e Madhe who had been burned before the bombing. So that I saw no similarities at all between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that this was the only bombing, the sole bombing, or was there some bombing before that as well?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: In the villages nearby - Krusha e Vogel, Krusha e Madhe, Nagafc - this was the only bombing and the last that we saw before leaving for Albania. We don't know what happened afterwards, and I can't say, but this was the first until that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the bombing began on the 24th of March, and there are 31 days in the month of March, which means that this was nine days into the bombing; it was the ninth day of the bombing. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: That's correct. But civilians have never been targeted, and there were 20.000 people over there. There was bombing of your forces. Your forces had been targeted, but not the civilian population. The only case upon a civilian population up until that moment was this one at Nagafc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you can see, the target here was the civilian population. And are you aware of the fact -- or rather, do you know of other cases, for example, of the bombing of columns of Albanian refugees carried out by NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is outside the scope of his evidence. It's not mentioned in his statement. What he says is that this was the first bombing, as far as he was concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevertheless, Your Honour, if you could allow me, I will reply. I haven't seen this, but I heard that the Serbian forces used the civilians as human shield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It only leads to an argument. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that the column of Albanian refugees bombed by NATO was something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's irrelevant, as far as this witness is concerned, and I'm going to stop that questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it clear from the statement made by this witness and his testimony here in Court when he says that the most tragic day of everything that he says in his statement was precisely that April 1st, when the bombing occurred at 2.00 a.m. in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't follow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear, in addition to the fact that our airplanes were not flying, that before that in your statement you explained the large presence of the army and the police in the area? Is that correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. I said in my statement that on the 25th of April [sic], one night after the start of the NATO bombing, the villages of Bellacerkva, Krusha e Madhe, Krusha e Vogel, and Celine and Nagafc were surrounded on all sides by a steel siege, and we heard these forces arriving from Gjakove, Prizren, Hoca e Madhe, and we were surrounded on all sides by large police and military forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a mistake in the transcript. It should be the 25th of March, not the 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long did those forces hold your village, have control of your village and the other villages that you mentioned were surrounded, as claim? For how many days did that go on?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I said in my statement that after the siege and intermittent shooting, the people withdrew from Krusha e Madhe because it's very close to the main road from Prizren to Gjakove. And I mentioned earlier that these forces passed from Celine to Nagafc through Krusha e Madhe, and we were in the streambed, and we could not see what was happening on the main road, but the forces were above us. And on the next day, when we went to Prroni i Cilave, we heard from the Serbian forces themselves that we couldn't go through Krusha because there were troops there. And we were entirely isolated in our houses until the day when we set off for Albania. So I cannot say what was going on round about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So throughout the time you were isolated by the army and the police or what you refer to as the Serbian forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The Serbian forces were always on the hills round about us. I've put it in my statement. And on the 28th, they entered the village. They entered the village and they looted us. And a soldier or a policeman got hold of me and said that, "We are on the hills round about." And this is how we were restricted in our movements. We were made aware that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They, in fact, blocked you. Now, apart from the fact that our planes were not flying, did it occur to you that during the night, at 2.00, that even if they were flying, they would not be able to bomb a terrain in which there were our forces on the ground as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not an answer he can give.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that it is quite clear what kind of bombing was afoot, even without that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that the only village with a Serb majority population in your area was Velika Hoca in the Orahovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes. Hoca e Madhe was indeed the only village with a Serbian majority population. But it also had the most weapons and the largest military and police presence. I know that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the course of the summer of 1998, in your municipality there was a great deal of violence and that, as can be seen from the OSCE reports, in that area there was a great deal of tension as they themselves state?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The mission was -- there was tension not only in these villages but throughout Kosova. The situation was very tense. But as far as I know, there had never been any military activity against Hoca e Madhe. There was no operation by the KLA against Hoca e Madhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the area of the Orahovac municipality, your area and your village, because you say you know the situation broader afield in Kosovo. So I'm sure that you know about the situation in the Orahovac municipality even better. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about the situation in Kosova, but I said that the situation was very tense throughout Kosova at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in your particular municipality during February 1999, that there was -- there were repeated clashes between the army and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: What time period are you talking about? Could you tell me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat. During February 1999, which means the period immediately prior to the events which you describe, that clashes became prevalent again between the army and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: With a full sense of responsibility, I can tell the Court that in the villages that I have been talking about so far, that is Krusha e Vogel, Krusha e Madhe, Nagafc, and Celine, I can say that there was no military activity. Whereas what happened on the front line between your forces and the KLA, I'm unable to say. But in the villages I have been talking about, there were no military operations and no provocations of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about your municipality, the municipality in which you lived. I assume that as a citizen and a physician communicating with many people, that you were aware of the situation in your municipality. Orahovac is a small municipality, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer that he knows of no KLA activity in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, judging by the book you received a moment ago, it says there that there were clashes once again in the Orahovac municipality. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... decide that. Did you know anything about the clashes in the municipality generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that we had no freedom of movement and we were isolated, how could we know what was happening in the municipality at large? We were cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As of what date were you isolated? When were you cut off?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: It's not a question of dates, but for years on end we didn't have the right to movement freely, because if we went out onto the main road, there would be police checkpoints and we would be mistreated. So we restricted our movements to a minimum and went out only for very pressing reasons. Otherwise, we didn't travel at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was the checkpoint, the police checkpoint, set up on that main road leading out of your village?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: There were always checkpoints, both in the direction of Prizren and the direction of Rahovec. But they increased, and the mistreatment increased after the clashes between your forces and the KLA. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that already in the summer of 1998, the summer of 1998, that there was a big clash between the KLA and our own forces, and that on the 17th of July, 1998, the KLA took control of Orahovac? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: We heard this from the many refugees who on that day came to our villages, nearby villages, and came to us out of fear. We heard about this from them, but otherwise I'm unable to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a battle, fighting in which the KLA took control of Orahovac. There was a lot of shooting. And as the KLA had taken control of Orahovac, what do you think your refugees were afraid of, the refugees that turned up in your village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment. The witness has said what he knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Malisevo, which is also in your municipality, was where the KLA had its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I would like to correct the accused here because Malisheva is not in our municipality but is a municipality in itself and is a long way from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You knew nothing about the headquarters of the KLA in Malisevo then?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I have heard that there was a KLA headquarters there, but I never was in Malisheva in this time, because to go there I would have had to go through Rahovec itself, and Malisheva was a long way away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in your particular municipality, the municipality of Orahovac, there were many cases, perhaps you at least know of some of these cases, of the abduction and killing of Albanians whom the KLA thought were inclined towards the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I don't know of any particular case, but I know very well that there are still 120 people missing from my people, that my cousin and a university professor is missing from my village. I do not know where these people are, but you are responsible for them, so you can tell us where these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked you about the many cases of people being abducted and killed, Albanians, people whom the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has given his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in passing, that is what it says in this book "As Seen, As Told." Precisely what I'm asking him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can put all of that in front of us in due course, but for the moment there's no point going on arguing with the witness. Now, you've had the hour which you were allowed. You can have another ten minutes because you were quicker with the last witness and there is quite a lot in this witness's evidence, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I saved a full 30 minutes of time with the last witness, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give you to the break. You can have quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in June 1998, in your own municipality, an Albanian was abducted who was well disposed towards the Serb authorities, and he was abducted in Brestovac by three KLA members. He was held in prison in Ratkovac. Do you know about that case? This is also mentioned in the OSCE documents here.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't read this document, but I don't know why you're so -- why you're so careful about this Albanian and not interested in all the others who have disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, would you just answer the questions. We'll get on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you bear in mind that I'm not asking you as the reader of a book but as a citizen of Orahovac and a physician at that who must have known what was going on in his municipality. Now, do you know when the KLA in your municipality killed two Albanians and a third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has given evidence about that. He said he didn't know of any particular case. Now, there's no point putting these matters to him when he says he doesn't know. As I've said, you can put your evidence before us in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you at least know of the daily protests on the part of families, of persons who were abducted and who had disappeared? Abducted at different times by the KLA and many of them later found dead.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I have never heard of these protests, and I don't think they took place. I did -- I heard very well of protests that were held by the Albanian side about the thousands of people of -- the thousands of Albanians who've disappeared, and no doubt you've heard about them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as this was something that was quite loud, you couldn't not hear it; do you know anything about the mortar attacks of the KLA on the village of Zociste, also in your municipality? In March 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: In March 1999, as I said before - I'll repeat it - we were unable to move. We were restricted in our movements. I know that at that time Zocishte was not inhabited by any Albanians because their houses were burned. The Albanian residents were refugees. So we couldn't go to Zocishte to find out what was happening there, so I don't know anything about what was going on beyond the villages I've mentioned. What was happening in Zocishte or Malisheva or Rahovec, I just cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the refugees from Zociste came to your own village, as far as I was able to understand you, and you mentioned refugees from Zociste.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I did not say in March 1999, but Albanian refugees from villages had been staying with us for over a year. They had left the village a long time before, because their houses had been burned down by their Serbian neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away is Bela Crkva from your village?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Bellacerkva is about 15 kilometres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you know anything about what was going on in Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Again, what time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely the period starting with the beginning of 1999, because KLA presence was in that village from then on.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: I have no idea that the KLA have ever been at the Bellacerkva or that there has been a KLA staff in there. Your information could be incorrect on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This information is correct, but we are not going to spend any more time on this. Are you aware of any one of these killings that were carried out by the KLA in your municipality? I'm going to read this out to you and you're going to tell me whether you know about any one of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You said earlier you didn't know of any particular cases. If the accused reads out a list to you, will you be able to answer or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because I don't know anybody. I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you about whether you had heard of any one of these killings, because there are a great many killings that were committed there by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's pointless to read out a list when he can't give an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He knows in advance that he does not know about any one of these killings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't know about any particular cases. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you can put this evidence before us in due course. It's pointless going on arguing with the witness. Now, is there anything else you want to ask him, anything new?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, for example, about the name of Muharrem Berisha, an Albanian, born in 1951, from Brestovac, from your municipality? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: How could I know everybody from other villages? You're talking about a village that is four villages apart from my own village. I can hardly know people from my own village, with about 6.000 people, let alone someone who lives about four villages apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if somebody is killed, then people usually hear about it, at least in the area where he lived. So you've never heard of him? And did you hear of Marko Gashi, another Albanian, born in 1927, from the village of Dobri Do, also from Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Are you aware how far Doberdoll is from my own village? And would you believe me that I've never been there, and I've got absolutely no idea which way it is located. If you start asking about all the honest Albanians, as you refer to them, as to who they are, I do not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why do you qualify these killed Albanians in that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was a comment. It's not taking us -- There's no need to answer. It's not taking us any further. Mr. Milosevic, you've had practically all the time. Unless you've got a new topic, I'm going to bring this examination to a close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have many questions that pertain to the crimes committed by the KLA, but obviously you do not seem to be willing to make it possible for questions of that nature to be put. I have a few pages of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have put them, you've heard the witness's answers, and I've said it's pointless to go on. You can put your evidence before us when it's your opportunity to do so. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you got any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I do have a few questions related to the statement that was read out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, in the second paragraph, Mr. Hoti, you said that in Velika Krusa there were about 6.000 people. After July 1998, this number increased because refugees had arrived from Retimlje, Zociste, and Opterusa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you give me an answer as to how many people came in that July of 1998, that summer of 1998, how many people came to your village?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: As you mentioned it, and I've written about it, about 3.000 to 4.000 refugees stayed with us in our village. It is approximately around that number. I can't give an exact figure. About 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I put the next question, Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to page 9 of the English version, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, in your statement, it says that the first Serb offensive took place in the spring of 1998. Is that correct? In the spring of 1998.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: It could be wrong through the translation. In the summer of 1998 and the offensive on Rahovec and its municipality. I'm referring to the summer - June, July - but not the spring of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a question of interpretation, but is that the time when these 3.000 or 4.000 people came to the village, to your village? Is that that particular time?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we understand each other now, then this offensive that you mentioned, does this offensive pertain to a clash between the KLA and the army of Yugoslavia, or the police, and that that is why these people primarily came to your village?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: For several times it was mentioned that there was an offensive in Rahovec and Bellacerkva, and the population, out of fear, fled and came to our village. All I know is that refugees reached our village and stayed with us throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have understood that part. But this offensive was launched against what, against whom? Was it aimed at driving these people out of their villages or was it aimed against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No. Against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another subject. I'm not going to go back to this, that Mr. Slobodan Milosevic read out, but again, it's page 7, of the English version, that is. In addition to everything that you have already confirmed while you were being examined by Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, I would like to go back to the third paragraph from the bottom. It says here that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. after this bombing that occurred that night, immediately during that night, you say: I came across a burned van where seven young men had fallen asleep -- had been sleeping. The young men were burned also. Does that mean that the van was not hit at all but that the young men in the van had burned?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The burning after the bombing of that van, the van was completely charred, and during the bombing, these youths were only buried after we returned from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm satisfied with your answer. That's not the way you had put it. But now for something else. The next day --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, Judge May, do I have a bit more time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That you said when you had set out for Prizren, that you took 15 wounded persons with you. "We put them on a truck and sent them to Prizren. Most of them had been mutilated by shrapnel." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: It may either be a mistake in translation or incorrect, because what I said is the night we set out for Prizren, a lorry, driven by an elderly person, was filled with some wounded people who were coming from several villages and headed towards the Prizren hospital, not with the population, but the lorry was filled at Nagafc with wounded people. It's only the driver who took the wounded people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not the way it's been explained here, but all right. This is the explanation you give now, and I'm not opposed to that explanation either. You said that that night in Nogavac, 40 to 50 people were killed.

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: That's correct. This can be corroborated with the reburial of all of them after our return from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain just one thing: That night you only heard the sound of aircraft, but you didn't see any aircraft?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: No, because one cannot see an aircraft at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first thing I wished to refer to. The second one: You were in a house. You heard detonations and you say that the window broke. But the house itself had not been hit; right? Is that right? I mean, it wasn't hit by a bomb?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: The house where me and my family were sheltered, and alongside another 80 persons, because of the tremors of the explosion by a grenade, or whatever it was - it was in the close vicinity - the roof was completely destroyed and the window panes were also shattered, but there was no burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this happened to many other houses too, right, due to the --

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: This happened to many, many houses at Nagafc. Almost all of Nagafc was completely destroyed that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Did you see, on the next day, before you set out - as you explained here, you were frightened - did you see any craters from these bombs next day in the village, and were they big? There were about ten of them. Were some of them 10 metres long and 7 metres wide? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: These craters, I did notice them even on the night when I set out to help the wounded, and I've seen the craters and I've seen -- because of the flames of the burning houses. On the very next day, before dawn, we set out for Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They were that big?

utterances.speaker: ALI HOTI
utterances.text: Yes, they were that big.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hoti, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If it please the Court, the Prosecution calls Rahim Latifi, spelled L-a-t-i-f-i, as our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I wonder if you could secure Exhibit 83, page 10, and put it on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Latifi, I understand, sir, that you were born in Pirana, is that correct, near Prizren, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you live there most of your life?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, all my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you look at the map that's on the ELMO. I don't know if that's displayed on the video screen. Do you see your town of Pirana on that map that's now before the Court?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes. It is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You're now pointing to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, on page 10 of Exhibit 83, there is a number 23 in the right-hand column. About two inches to the left of that is Pirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You're pointing to Pirana now, thank you, on the screen. Thank you. And that's in the municipality of Prizren, is it?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, the municipality of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You can -- that's -- Sir, I understand that you took your secondary education in Prizren, and you studied agriculture for some time at the university. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Four children.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you, in 1998 and 1999, live with your parents and another brother in the same house with your family in the village of Pirana?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would now propose if I may, Your Honours, to give a very brief skeleton summary of what is contained in the witness's statement, but before I do, I should ask him some questions about that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, were you interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 28th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you gave that statement. And was that statement subsequently translated into Albanian and given to you to review on the 29th of January, 2002, of this year?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you appear before a presiding officer at that time and indicate that the contents of that statement were true to the best of your knowledge and belief at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that statement now be tendered as the next exhibit in these proceedings, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit number 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: While that statement is being distributed, I propose, with the Court's permission, to read a brief skeleton summary. I've made, actually, a copy of it for the benefit of the translators, and I believe a copy has also been handed to all the parties. In the statement, Your Honours, he describes incidents in the spring of 1998 when he found three dead villagers. All of them had been shot in the back of the head. One had his hands tied with a metal string, behind his back. Another's body was black and blue from having been beaten. All were civilians. He describes that on the 24th of March, 1999, in the evening, the NATO started its air campaign. And by 4.00 of the next day, the 25th of March, 1999, his village was surrounded by the army and MUP units, by tanks, various military vehicles, and a lot of personnel. At 8.00 in the morning, the first house in Pirana was set on fire, and at approximately the same time, the Serbs started shelling the village. Later, the police burned the whole village to the ground. According to his statement, when the attack on the village began, the residents started to evacuate. There was a free corridor to Mamusha village, so 80 per cent of the population of the village, which he estimated to be about 1.900, started moving towards Mamusha. The rest of the population, including the witness, went towards Srbica. On the way to Srbica, a sniper killed one villager and wounded another. In the village of Srbica, some Serb families met the refugees and asked the police that they not be harmed, but next day, about 70 police started shooting at their tractors. Some Serb residents tried to protect them from the police. And the witness's family stayed there for over a month. About three weeks later, the chief of police of Prizren came and said that whoever was not originally from Srbica village should leave the village and go to Albania. The local Serbs from Srbica then organised six buses for the refugees, but the witness and his family of 86 members stayed in Srbica for ten days longer because there was no room for them in the buses. On the 25th of April, 1999, the Serbs started a big offensive in the area of Srbica. From Srbica area, they would shell the villages of Pirana, Reti e Ulet, Reti, and Randobrava. On the 26th of April, his family hired a bus for about 2.000 German marks and they were escorted out of the village by local Serbs. They proceeded with the cars both in front and behind the bus until they reached the village of Zhur. At the border crossing at Morina, their personal documents were taken away. Now, the witness also describes several incidents in his statement about bodies that he saw, and there are some eight of them. First of all, in a dry stream near Pirana, the police buried several bodies with a bulldozer. Secondly, one day he saw two police trucks on the road from Krusha with many bodies inside, but he doesn't know where they took them. Three, he describes an incident where he reburied three bodies in Pirana. Four, he describes an incident in the village of Randobrava where a shell hit a tractor and a convoy and all six members of a family got killed. Five, in the same village, he found the body of a man about 45 to 47 years old whose fingers were cut off and his abdomen was cut open. Six, in the village of Reti e Ulet, he describes a gravesite where he helped bury 25 people who came from the village of Krusha e Madhe. Seven, he also found 12 more bodies in Randobrava that they buried in the field. And finally, number eight, he describes finding 52 people killed in the houses in the village of Velika Krusa, most with gunshot wounds to the head. That is a very brief skeletal summary and I have no further questions at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, may I make a correction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srbica, it is called Srbica but not Skenderaj. Skenderaj is not near our territory where I live. It's a technical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That must have been a translation, because I do not recall using the word "Skenderaj." It certainly is not contained in the skeleton statement that I read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you graduated from high school in Prizren and that you attended the faculty of agriculture for two years in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you enrolled in secondary school; which years? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from secondary school in 1987; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you enrol in the faculty of agriculture; which year?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In 1990, in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you leave the faculty of agriculture?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why did you abandon your studies at the university?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Because our university was closed and I didn't have the right conditions to continue in private houses. Because after the university was closed, classes continued to be held in and among private houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you know that at the university in Pristina, there was a faculty of agriculture all the time?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: It's true, there was, but only for Serbs and people who accepted your regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could Albanians freely study at the faculty of agriculture at the University of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: When are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that period from 1992 onwards, when you left the university.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't free.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that a large number of Albanians did study at the faculty of agriculture in Pristina after 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, among private houses. Not on the faculty premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's just clear this up. It is your claim that the Albanians did not study at the regular faculty of agriculture of the University of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: This question is not clear to me. I tried to study in premises because to get the right conditions, but the truth is that we were evicted from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If I have understood your answer correctly, Albanians were evicted from the faculty of agriculture in Pristina, and from 1992 onwards, you say that there weren't any Albanian students at the faculty of agriculture of the University of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: On the premises of the faculty, there weren't. In private houses, in rooms 4 metres square, there were, but they didn't have access to a library or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Therefore, I understand that you said that at the regular faculty of agriculture of the university in Pristina, from 1992 onwards, there were no Albanian students. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I can repeat again: On the faculty premises, the premises of the agricultural faculty, there were no Albanian students, but there were among private houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. When you say "among private houses," this did not belong to the faculty itself; this was some kind of parallel studies. So nobody was studying at the university any longer?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: You can't call it parallel. We tried -- that is, our students, our professors, we were trying not to leave students on the streets. You can't study in private houses like you can in university premises, and even among private houses, our students were harassed and persecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, they were harassed and persecuted?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Everywhere: on the streets, in their flats, at the bus station, in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who persecuted them?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Uniformed policemen mainly, civilians. There was no way we could protect ourselves from the police. You couldn't bring your faculty identity card home. If they found you with a faculty identity card, you were in trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were any students arrested? Or let me be more precise: What did this persecution consist of?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: All kinds of things. There's no dispute about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But describe at least some of these forms of persecution, when you say that students were persecuted in Pristina or in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In April 1992, in Aktash II, seven students, friends of mine, were arrested. They were mistreated until they lost consciousness, on the street and then in the police station. There's a short description for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how long were they detained in the police station?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: About 24 hours. Just because of these 24 hours, they had to interrupt their studies for two months, because of the way they were beaten and mistreated. Whether they were women or men, the question was: Are you a student? Are you studying? They were concerned to brainwash us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, claim that it was the police that prevented Albanian students from going to their studies, from studying?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The police received orders from somewhere and obstructed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, at that time, the time that you're talking about, how many Albanian students were enrolled at the regular university in Pristina, as regular students?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I only know about my faculty. In the first year, there were 120 students, and in the second, the number was reduced. Merely in the arable department. I can't talk about the rest of the university. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At the second year, the number is reduced anyway, minus those students that don't complete the first year. Was that the reason or was there some other reason?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I was a good student. I passed all my exams on time. I am talking about myself as an example. But what worried us most of all was the treatment of the girls, because they were unable to travel from Prizren to Pristina because of the maltreatment, and we had to protect them because of our honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who abused girls?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The police. Who else? The civilians were not authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you quote an example of the police abusing some girls?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: For example, two girls from Suhareke got off at Stimlje and were maltreated, but they didn't come with us in the bus. We had to leave them there. And then what happened to them, I don't know. I don't know who they were. I just know that they came from the Suhareke area. I don't know which faculty they were studying at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You lived in Prizren, in a town in which there were Albanians, Serbs, and Turks alike, and also a number of Roma; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the time you're talking about, in the Prizren municipality, were there Albanians and Serbs and Turks and Romas holding responsible positions?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In the recent years, I don't know of there having been any Albanians. There were reduced number of Turks, and I don't think there were any Roma, and the majority were Serbs. All the managers were changed at that time, all the employers, all the supervisors, all the bosses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Sokol Qyshi from Prizren, for example?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He's an Albanian. I assume you know him because his name -- you can judge that by his name. And he was a director in Prizren throughout that time, right up until the war. Do you know about that? Do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: From his name, he's an Albanian, but I didn't work in the administration. I had no way of knowing him. This is the first time I've heard of his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, his name just came to mind, but I have a number of other names, Albanian and Turkish, who held responsible functions. Now, did it occur to you, in view of the structure of the authorities in Prizren municipality, which was composed of Serbs, Albanians and Turks, that for the incidents that you spoke about, that you asked their assistance, that is to say that you appealed to the authorities in the municipality for their help? And it was a municipality that had representatives of both the Serbs, Albanians, and Turks.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: What sort of aid should I be looking for? I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: If there were certain incidents that took place against people from Prizren, those of you who were studying, did it ever occur to you to go to your own municipality, the municipality of Prizren, and go to one of the functionaries in the municipality who was an Albanian or a Turk or a Serb, whatever, to report to them that something had been going on that was not normal and proper, that was out of order? Did it ever occur to you to report that to them?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: We did think of this, but we didn't follow it up. We went into the police station, and our farewell was, "I hope you -- God willing you'll come out alive. And if you don't, you get buried."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: That's the sort of thing that happened. This is not just rumour. Anybody who went to the police station, that sort of thing happened. You had no one to complain to, because we had a -- a parallel municipal authority in which the Albanians were predominant. But we had -- we had no reason to go to these police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next part of your statement. I don't understand that if something happens to you that you don't go and report it or complain to somebody about that. I don't quite seem to understand that.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: That's how it was. That's how it was. There was no one to complain to. And if you did complain, nobody paid you any attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you did not complain. So you don't know if anybody would have paid you any attention or not. You didn't try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that in the spring of 1998, you found three dead farmers, Mehmet Elshani, his son Afrim, and a worker of theirs, Sali Gashi.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they were liquidated by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I don't know who they were killed by. What I'm saying is we found them killed. I don't know who killed them, because it happened at night. They were killed at about 10.00 at night. We heard the gunshots. And it was impossible for us to emerge out of our houses at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that from the autumn of 1998 onwards, as far as I was able to understand, the situation calmed down, relatively speaking, and that there were no major incidents.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: There was -- forces were preparing. Military and police forces were rotating and deploying, especially the army. So they were not dealing with the local population. It was quite obvious that they were preparing. They were just swapping locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were they preparing for?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I do not know. You should know this better. You should be aware of the tactics better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the evening of the 24th of March, air -- the air campaign started, and that in the early hours of the morning on the 25th of March, your village was surrounded by the army and Serbian police units with tanks, various military vehicles, and a lot of personnel, as you say in your statement. Now, where were you surrounded?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: We were surrounded on the 25th of March. The noise of the tanks and other heavy vehicles could be heard since early on in the morning at 4.00, whereas movement within the village started at about 8.00 when the burning, shelling, uncontrolled, indiscriminate, started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What village are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Pirana. Pirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far is Pirana away from Prizren?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Eleven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see from Pirana the bombing of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Prizren was not bombed from Pirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean bombed from Pirana but bombed from the air by NATO.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: You can only see a little. I understand. I understand. But there's very little leeway because Prizren is on high ground and Pirana is not. So very little can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the incident you describe. You say that at the same time, they started setting houses on fire and shelling the village -- and shelled the village. How was it possible for them to be in the village and set fire to the houses and at the same time to throw shells on that village and burn the houses, as you say?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: They set fire to the houses by hand from the vicinity, not from Prizren. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Prizren. I'm talking about on the spot. You say that they were setting houses on fire and shelling the villages at the same time. If they are setting fire to the houses, it means that they are in the village. If they are shelling the village, then they are shelling the village that they were in. Now, how is that possible? How can these two things take place at the same time simultaneously? How can they be in the village setting fire to the houses and shell the village from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The shelling did not occur at the same time as the police forces entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about this because you say in your statement that it occurred at the same time. You say, "Approximately at the same time," et cetera. And later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It ought to be read --.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It ought to be in context. "At 8.00, the first house in Pirana was set on fire. This was the house," and the name is given. "Approximately at the same time, the Serbs started shelling the village." Now, that's the context in which it's put. And in fact, it goes on: "There was no damage. I saw later the police burnt down to the ground the whole village."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But you must put the whole statement to the witness so that he can -- it can be dealt with fairly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that I have supplied the essence, the substance of it, because in the statement, it says that the house was set on fire, too, and the village shelled at the same time. So that was what my question referred to. But that's just a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the next day, you went to Donja Srbica and that the Serb population in the village helped you to find your way and go into the houses, and you say that your family stayed in the village for one month.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Not on the morrow but on -- because the day after that was the 26th, and this happened on the 25th. And we left the house at 8.00. We headed towards Srbica. And in that convoy, Xhafer Elshani was killed. Mehmet Elshani was wounded. And we lay down on the ground for over two hours until we started heading towards the village. Local Serbs prepared us for staying in local villages, in the local village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was asking you. Your family stayed in the village for a whole month, as you say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Yes, for a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During that time, did anybody mistreat you in any way, or did anything to harm you, or was rude to you?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In Srbica, this did not happen, as did in other places like Krusha e Vogel, where Serbian inhabitants lived as well. In Srbica, it was a bit different. There was partial provocation, but they were not of the extent that it endangered one's life. But certain Serbs and Albanians who could have been able to cohabit even today, but it was only the war that marked the parting of the ways, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that what you said is quite correct, and that is that the war was the cause of all this. You said: The police kept coming, but they did not harm us. The police would come but do no harm to us. That's what you said. You said that the Serbs from Donja Srbica later organised six buses for you to help you be able to seek shelter.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I do not know how this came to pass. From Prizren, from the municipality, six, seven buses came to Srbica and told us to leave because our life was in danger. Your police and army -- from your police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The first group left for Albania, or set off for Albania, and we later learned that they had made it, whilst we stayed in Srbica for another three weeks, the rest, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you describe an event on the 25th of April, when a big offensive started. You say the Serbs started a big offensive in the area of Donja Srbica, and from Donja Srbica, they would shell the villages of Pirana, Retimlje, Randubrava, et cetera. Do you know of any KLA presence in the area, and do you know what was happening in the area with respect to the clashes that were going on between the army and police, on the one side, and the KLA, on the other?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No, we were not aware of what was happening, but we could only see the shelling, police, Serbs, and the infantry assaulting these villages. That part of those villages that had escaped the burning of the 25th, 26th, 27th of March was burnt on that very same day. I am not aware of what pretext or excuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about any pretext. I'm just asking you whether you are aware of the present course of events and the attack on the police and army by the KLA in that area.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any KLA there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you're from those parts, do you know, in October 1998, when about -- when the KLA killed a soldier? His name was Srdjan Simonovic, and he was killed precisely in those parts where you come from.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I do not know. I have not heard of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about another case, when, on the 17th of March, 1999 - that means that the Verification Mission of the OSCE was still there, they were still on the ground - that another soldier, by the name of Vladimir Markovic, was also killed, also in your area?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that in the village of Pirana, in actual fact, on the 27th of March, 1999, that a soldier by the name of Bojan Jovanovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: At that time, I was not staying in the village, and I do not know who has been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the next village, the village of Landovica, on the previous day, soldier Slobodan Gasparic was killed. Did you hear about that killing?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here -- it says here that during the time you were still in your village in the Prizren municipality -- I have here a fairly long list of soldiers who were killed. Now, I'm not going to read it out to you and ask you the individual names, but let me just ask you generally: Did you hear, throughout the time that you spent in the area, about the killing of any soldier at all, soldier or policeman, in the Prizren municipality, either in your village or in the neighbouring villages, or did you hear about anything similar happening? So any of these events or anything similar happening. And the press, radio, television broadcast this. It was on Radio Prizren in Albanian, Turkish, and Serbian. But tell me, did you hear of any of these events?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The media at the time worked under restricted conditions. There was no information on true events. There was disinformation. Even what was broadcast, we did not take that to be resembling the truth, but simply misinformation. It was not our media, because if it had been ours, it would have been like the ones that we have at this very particular moment, and we have not followed the media of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And once again in the village of Pirana, do you happen to know of another event? It was the killing of a policeman by the name of Zvezdan Tasic and it took place in April, the time you're talking about. Were you there then?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: When the burial of Zvezdan occurred -- and I've known him personally. He was an unusual criminal in our areas, not only in our areas, but elsewhere as well. When he was buried, we were in Srbica, and we were scared, because when we saw police on four buses, we were not aware of why they were there. When we heard that Zvezdan had been killed, that's when we heard what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you just heard about that one killing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: At that time we were staying in the village, and I lived near the cemetery, so that we were kind of participants over there and we had heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from him, you didn't hear about the killing of any other Serb, whether policeman or soldier?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this man, Zvezdan Tasic, who was killed, he was a policeman. Why do you refer to him and call him a criminal?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: That's what he was. We had heard that at the Rahovec clash he had wreaked havoc, and that's why I call him a criminal. If he had been alive, he'd be here with you, because there were people who had known him, because he served in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know also that all these present-day leaders - Thaci, the Selimi brothers, Cekve [phoen], et cetera - are criminals as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's a general comment. No need to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you do not know about the killing of a single Serb, I'm going to read out to you the names of a few Albanians who were killed in your area. So now we are going to see whether you know of any one of them. You knew about this one personally, but have you ever heard of the killing of any one of these: Marjan Doni, Bojaxhiu Fatmir, Dejcaj Binak, Ponik Arsim, Cemaj [phoen] Beha, Likaj [phoen] Hamit, Rijazit [phoen] Avdyl, Morina Sali?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will do for the moment. The witness is to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the killing of any one of these persons whose names I've just read out, that were committed by the KLA? These are Albanians, first and foremost, and this was precisely in your area.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: I have never known any of these people. I didn't know them, and I have no information about how they were killed, or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about whether you knew them; I'm asking about whether you heard about the killing of these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's mentioned that he has no information about how they were killed. It's alleged -- just a moment. It's alleged they were killed by the KLA. No doubt other names are about to be read out to you with the same allegation attached. Can you help us as to that? Do you know anything about this at all, these allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's pointless to go on reading out the names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I should not ask any more about any one of these killings that had taken place where the witness was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about an event -- I mean, I'm asking you about this because, if I understood your assertion correctly, you've been saying that you did not know anything about any KLA activity whatsoever, at any time.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In our villages, in the places where we were staying in Pirana and Srbica, there were no KLA soldiers. I never saw them. So I can't comment on things I haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you know about this, whether you've heard of this, because you've been talking about a great many things that you've only heard of, not seen. Have you heard of KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: It's not true that I've been talking about things I know from hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I am asking you. Have you heard of any KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: No. I had no connection, either direct or indirect, with the KLA, and I never heard about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's pointless to go on asking about the KLA of this witness, so you should move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question related to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you at least heard of a big event, in terms of the numbers involved, between the 13th and 14th of December, 1994, when almost 100 members of the KLA in the region of Prizren, on the border, clashed with the army that were manning the border? A number were killed, a number were arrested, and also a large quantity of ammunition, weapons, materiel were taken. Do you remember at least that incident that had to do with the KLA in your area?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: The border area is not near my village. It's a very long way away. There's no way I could hear of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is an incident that was talked about a great deal, and I had assumed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that together with 20 people, you buried the bodies of the killed persons from Velika Krusa. Who are these people that you did this with?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: In the evening - I'll say it as it originally happened - that a child's voice came to us and we had the idea that we would put ourselves at risk because perhaps there were children left by themselves in the fields. And we saw many corpses near the Randobrava in the fields, in Krusha e Madhe. They were terribly, terribly badly -- they were wounded in the head. They were burned. They -- they were -- there was no one to bury them. There were some cousins of mine, and there were some civilians who had been left behind in Randobrava and Krusha e Madhe, and that's how we did this job together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not see who killed these people and how?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: We know who killed them. They were your troops. But how they were killed, well, we saw the corpses. They were killed in the most cruel fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the KLA took pictures of the graves and the corpses.

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: On that day in the evening, we accidentally met in Randobrava two uniformed soldiers. They were also armed. And they had come out to reconnoiter the territory with the same idea, that there should not be unburied bodies left on the ground. And we told them about this event. And we handed over these photographs because we were scared to have them in our pockets, because -- because for the sake of a photograph, we would put our lives and our entire families in danger. How would we put ourselves at risk for the sake of a photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I've been asking you. Quite simply, I'm putting the following question to you: You were in contact, therefore, with the representatives of the KLA. So far, you've been saying that you had never had any contact with them whatsoever and that you had never heard of any kind of KLA activity. Did you encounter anyone else? Did you talk to anyone else? Did you have any other contacts with the KLA except for these two that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: It was a very fleeting contact, accidental. On that day it happened, but never again. And when I came back from Albania, I saw them again. But it was a very fleeting contact on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to clarify this in view of what you've written. And in Velika Krusa, you did not see who had killed these people and how?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Who killed them? I told you. They were your forces, because this was an act of revenge because of NATO. And after the bombing started, this action of vengeance on the part of the army and the police started, because we were defenseless. We had no army. It was vengeance against the civilian population. It was murder, rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just awhile ago you said that you would not speak of anything that you had not seen, of anything that you had only heard about, but this that you've just said is something that you've only heard about. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: These are things we experienced, not things we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked you whether you saw who had killed these people, and you had not seen anyone. But you claim that it was, as you had put it, the Serb troops that had done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer about this. Mr. Milosevic, we should try and finish this witness today since we're not sitting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can finish with this witness, because I have other questions related to victims in the area. However, since the witness answered that he did not know absolutely a thing about them, I think it's pointless to ask him, because he said that he knew nothing about any kind of KLA activity. There is no need for me to ask him anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then just one more thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not have an army. And just a few minutes ago you said that you encountered these two soldiers. These two soldiers that you encountered, did they belong to this army, the KLA, that you consider to be your own army, or did they belong to someone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with that. Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions for this witness? Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just one, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked by the accused about the organisation of the six buses when you left Srbica. Did you want to leave for Albania?

utterances.speaker: RAHIM LATIFI
utterances.text: Nobody ever leaves their own home of their own free will, but it was a question of saving our families, because our houses were being burnt. Murders were starting. We thought the same thing would happen to us, because that -- we were thinking that NATO was our rescue, and then this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Latifi, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, will you be calling the witnesses in the order on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is our proposal, health and everything else and availability, but, yes, we intend to call the witnesses as -- as scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can make our preparations. We're not sitting tomorrow because there's a Plenary, a meeting of the Judges, but we shall be sitting again on Wednesday, when? If I'm right, the time is 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And we have the extended hours then to 4.00? 9.30 to 4.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will sit into the afternoon. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of April, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
